items.headline: SpaceX flies 700th Falcon 9, adding 27 Starlink satellites
items.title: SpaceX closes out October with Halloween eve Falcon 9 launch, 700th Falcon 9 launch to date
items.scifi_hook: SpaceX marks its 700th Falcon 9 launch, boosting the internet constellation on Halloween eve.
items.eli5: A reusable rocket lifted off from California and landed its booster back on a ship after deploying 27 satellites.
items.why: More satellites improve global broadband coverage and demonstrate rapid launch turnaround.
items.text: The Starlink 15-18 mission lifts off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Oct. 30, 2026, local time. Image: SpaceX. Update: Oct. 31, 12:25 a.m. EDT (0425 UTC): SpaceX landed its first stage booster on the droneship. SpaceX capped off the month of October with the launch of a Starlink mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Friday night. The flight was the 700th launch of a Falcon 9 rocket to date. The Starlink 15-18 mission on the eve of Halloween will add another 27 broadband internet satellites to the company’s low Earth orbit constellation. Liftoff from Space Launch Complex 4 East happened at 9:04 p.m. PDT (12:04 a.m. EDT / 0404 UTC). The rocket flew on a southeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad. SpaceX launched the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number 1093. This was its 18th flight following the launches of Transporter-16, two missions for the Space Development Agency, and 14 batches of Starlink satellites. Nearly 8.5 minutes after liftoff, B1093 landed on the droneship, Of Course I Still Love You , positioned in the Pacific Ocean. This was the 231st landing on this vessel and the 675th Falcon booster landing to date. Winding down Falcon, ramping up Starship The launch on the eve of Halloween was SpaceX’s 11th and final orbital flight in October. items.headline: NASA seeks commercial proposals to rescue Hubble telescope
items.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
items.scifi_hook: NASA invites companies to devise a way to lift or safely retire the aging Hubble space observatory.
items.eli5: NASA wants ideas from firms to boost Hubble’s orbit or guide it to a controlled re‑entry before it falls back to Earth.
items.why: Extending Hubble’s life preserves a unique scientific asset and avoids uncontrolled debris.
items.text: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. items.headline: Uranium stocks tumble despite higher long‑term fuel prices
items.title: Uranium shares slide even as analysts see tighter supply
items.scifi_hook: Uranium shares slide as investors worry about tighter supply and financing hurdles for new mines.
items.eli5: Even though nuclear fuel prices are strong, uranium company stocks fell because funding and permits are hard to get.
items.why: Lower valuations could delay new uranium production, affecting future nuclear power growth.
items.text: Stocks of uranium companies are falling despite the strongest long-term fuel prices in more than 18 years, as investors weigh an expected tightening of supply against rising costs and the difficulty of bringing new projects into production. The VettaFi Global Uranium Mining Index, a benchmark tracking uranium mining shares worldwide, dropped 16% in September and the Nasdaq Sprott Junior Uranium Miners Index lost 22%, while spot uranium prices barely moved. Financial-market pressures appear to be overwhelming an improving fuel-market outlook, Sprott market strategist Paul Wong wrote in an Oct. 28 analysis . “Even if the expected uranium price is unchanged, tighter liquidity can raise the cost of capital, compress valuation multiples and delay the market’s recognition of future project value,” Wong wrote. “Those effects are real, but they are cyclical and financial.” The divergence matters because stronger fuel prices alone cannot deliver new production: developers still need permits, financing and years of construction. Sprott manages the world’s largest physical uranium fund, Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (TSX: U.UN; U.U), which held $7.6 billion in net assets as of Thursday. Spot prices Spot uranium prices are forecast to average $95 per lb. next year, up from an expected $88 this year, analysts at Fitch Solutions’ BMI wrote in an Oct. 15 outlook. items.headline: Nord Quantique demonstrates error‑corrected qubit in a single cavity
items.title: Julien Camirand Lemire (Nord Quantique): One Cavity, One Error-Corrected Qubit
items.scifi_hook: A Canadian startup shows a qubit that corrects its own errors using microwave photons inside one cavity.
items.eli5: The company uses light particles trapped in a tiny box to fix mistakes in quantum bits without needing many extra qubits.
items.why: Improved error correction is key to building scalable quantum computers.
items.text: Julien Camirand Lemire, co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique , is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Julien discusses Nord Quantique ‘s bosonic code approach, which uses microwave photons in superconducting cavities to achieve quantum error correction without large qubit overhead, including their GKP and Tesseract code demonstrations and a quantum error correction gain that has more than doubled since 2024. They explore the company’s roadmap toward 10^-7 to 10^-9 error rates by 2032, the four-qubit system entering operation this year, and how Quebec’s Sherbrooke ecosystem has enabled a capital-efficient build. They also discuss high-rate codes, transmon-based scaling challenges, and much more. Transcript Yuval: Hello, Julien, thank you for being here. items.headline: Radical AI builds autonomous labs to fast‑track alloy creation
items.title: Radical AI uses autonomous labs to accelerate alloy discovery
items.scifi_hook: A self‑driving lab uses AI and robots to spin out hundreds of new metal recipes in weeks.
items.eli5: AI guides robots to mix and test metal formulas, finding alloys that need fewer rare metals.
items.why: It helps US makers cut dependence on China‑controlled minerals.
items.rationale: AI‑driven alloys could boost US supply chain.
items.text: As the United States pushes to reduce its dependence on China for critical minerals, New York-based Radical AI is taking a different approach to securing strategic materials: using artificial intelligence to develop new alloys that require fewer supply-constrained metals. The company has developed a self-driving laboratory platform that uses AI and robotics to design, manufacture and test advanced materials, an innovation that it says dramatically shortens the discovery process for alloys used in aerospace, defense and other industrial applications. In September, Radical AI partnered with Sandia National Laboratories to perform research on metal-hydrogen interactions and discover new materials to separate hydrogen from waste gas streams. Working from its facility at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, Radical AI has demonstrated an alloy discovery process that produced 300 new compositions in approximately 16 weeks, CEO Joseph Frause told MINING.COM in an interview. items.headline: Researchers create molecular cage that traps shape‑matched planar molecules
items.title: 'Molecular armor' can trap shape-matched planar molecules
items.scifi_hook: A tiny cage built from curved molecules snaps shut on matching flat guests.
items.eli5: Scientists linked two curved, light‑absorbing molecules to form a pocket that catches flat molecules that fit exactly.
items.why: It opens new ways to capture and store specific chemicals.
items.text: A research team has designed and synthesized a molecular cage with an internal cavity by connecting two curved π-conjugated molecules face-to-face at three points.
